clue.text: Leading question that begins court proceedings?

definitions.text: Leading question that begins court proceedings?

parts.words: Leading question that begins court proceedings
parts.note: surface reading: a barrister's leading question opening a trial in a court of law
setter's reading: the court is a tennis court, and the question is the jaunty invitation that starts a game

explanation.surface: A lawyer opens a trial with a loaded question to a witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading question' and 'court' both pull towards law; the court is for tennis, and the question is the stock invitation to play, a catchphrase of old drawing-room comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the classic invitation to a game, so it is literally a question that starts play on a tennis court.

clue.text: Discovery perhaps underpinning early man's male attribute

indicators.note: in a down clue, something underpinning sits beneath, so this piece is written after the other

parts.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis, with the possessive
Discovery is a variety of English eating apple

explanation.surface: An archaeological find props up evidence of something typical of early man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovery' suggests a find, but it is an apple variety; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adam's apple is the laryngeal bulge in the throat, usually more prominent in men, hence a male feature.

clue.text: Book in which you found firm or faint-hearted servants

definitions.text: Book in which you found firm

parts.note: yellow means cowardly
pages are young servants or attendants

explanation.surface: A directory where you once looked up a business, or a band of timid retainers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole first half; 'or' offers the wordplay as an alternative route to the same answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow Pages was the printed business telephone directory where you looked up companies by trade.

clue.text: Blade grabbed by an ego out of control — keep out of it!

indicators.note: what is grabbed is held inside, so this piece goes within the other letters
something out of control is in disorder, so the letters scatter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged
the blade of a rowing oar, used for the whole oar

explanation.surface: A sword seized by a raging egotist, with a warning to stay clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The blade stands for the whole oar it belongs to; the exclamation is the definition, the warning a sign on such a place gives.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area is a place one must not enter, so 'keep out of it!' is the warning it carries.

clue.text: Big group of animals, filled with energy, brought into the world

parts.note: fat as in large, bulky

indicators.note: something filled with an item holds it inside, so that letter goes within

parts.note: a herd is a group of cattle or similar
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A large herd, full of vigour, has been born.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big group of animals' reads as one phrase, but it splits in two: 'Big' and 'group of animals'.
explanation.definitionFit: To father a child is to beget it, so a fathered child is one brought into existence by its sire.

clue.text: Agaric's cap seen below river bank hardly ever

indicators.note: in a down clue, being below means coming after in the written entry

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river

indicators.note: a cap sits on top, so in a down clue it means the opening letter of the word

parts.note: the first letter of the mushroom name
to bank on someone is to rely on them

explanation.surface: A mushroom's top appears on a riverbank only seldom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like the riverside in the scene; it is the verb, as in 'bank on'. An agaric is a gilled mushroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarely means seldom, which is the same as almost never.

clue.text: Fur tucked into denim requires being shown up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top
something tucked into the following words is concealed within their run of letters

parts.note: the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Fur sewn into denim must be displayed, a fashion note.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the white winter coat of the stoat, prized as a trimming on robes.

clue.text: Sister only occasionally unfunny

indicators.note: taking something only now and then means picking every other letter rather than all

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A sister who is just now and then lacking in humour.
explanation.definitionFit: A nun is addressed as Sister, the title for a woman in a religious order.

clue.text: Runner going through hell persists, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the spelling is decided by sound alone

parts.note: to stick at something is to persist

explanation.surface: An athlete who keeps going through a gruelling ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete; in crosswords it often means a river, flowing through the underworld here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Styx is the river of the Greek underworld, which the dead were ferried across.

clue.text: Gorilla eats peeled bananas, fierce creature

indicators.note: going bananas is going crazy, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: peeling strips the skin, so the outer letters go and only the middle stays

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A fierce ape tucks into bananas with the skins off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the gorilla's food and 'eats' like its action, but one stirs the letters and the other is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An alligator is a large and dangerous reptile, a fair example of a fierce animal.

clue.text: Sole coated with crumbs is ready

indicators.note: a coating wraps around, so the second piece surrounds the first

parts.note: crumbs and my are both mild exclamations of surprise
sole means single, only one

explanation.surface: A fish fillet in breadcrumbs is cooked and ready to serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ready' is British slang for cash, and 'crumbs!' is a mild exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'. 'Sole' looks like the fish but means only.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The ready' is informal for available cash, so ready stands for money.

clue.text: Wise person taking to whiskey in room on ship

indicators.note: a person taking something holds it, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: a sage is a wise person
taken as written
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A wise old soul turns to whisky in his cabin aboard ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowage is the space available for storing cargo or belongings on a vessel.

clue.text: Behind large pub, film bird

indicators.note: behind means following, so the final piece comes after the others

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
an inn is a pub
E.T. is the Spielberg film

explanation.surface: Out the back of a big pub, someone films a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The linnet is a small brown finch, common across Britain.

clue.text: Unusual place with no exit needs rebuilding

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the parts back together in a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd building with no way out has to be reconstructed.
explanation.definitionFit: Exceptional means out of the ordinary, which is what unusual means.

clue.text: Eyes teary, upset about Romeo long ago

definitions.note: adverbial phrase; the answer is a noun for times past, as in 'the songs of long ago'

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece
upset means knocked over, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Tearful and distressed about a lover, thinking back to the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romeo' pulls towards a lost lover in the scene, but it is just the letter R.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesteryear means the past, time gone by, which is what long ago refers to.

clue.text: Scattered pennies gathered by fellow editor

indicators.note: things gathered by someone are held within their arms, so they go inside

parts.note: a peer is an equal, a fellow
p is a penny, doubled for the plural
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A colleague and an editor pick up loose change strewn about.
explanation.definitionFit: Peppered means sprinkled or dotted about, as in a text peppered with errors.

clue.text: Some letters in Kerouac memoir a high point

indicators.note: only some of the letters are taken, a run concealed in the words that follow

parts.note: the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Parts of Jack Kerouac's memoir mark the peak of his writing.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the peak or summit of achievement, the highest point.

clue.text: Detectives experience antipathy

parts.note: DIs are Detective Inspectors
to taste something is to experience it, as in tasting defeat

explanation.surface: Police detectives encounter hostility.
explanation.definitionFit: Distaste is a feeling of dislike or aversion, much the same as antipathy.

clue.text: Gloomy squad briefly leaves for refreshment

indicators.note: cutting something brief drops its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: black as in a black mood
a squad is a team

explanation.surface: A downcast team walks off the pitch to get a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as the squad departing; it links wordplay to definition, with a nod to tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Black tea, a cup without milk, is a common drink taken to refresh oneself.

clue.text: Peg and hoop making toy for children

parts.note: peg is informal for leg
O is round like a hoop

explanation.surface: A peg and a hoop are put together as a simple plaything.
explanation.definitionFit: Lego is the brand of interlocking plastic building bricks played with by children.

clue.text: Only a small population here in work?

definitions.text: Only a small population here in work?

parts.words: Only a small population here in work
parts.note: surface reading: a place where few people have jobs
setter's reading: a population of tiny people, found in a literary work, Swift's Gulliver's Travels

explanation.walkthrough: 'In work' suggests employment; it means within a book, where the island's inhabitants are only six inches tall.
explanation.definitionFit: The island visited by Gulliver in Swift's satire is peopled by tiny folk, so its population is literally small.

clue.text: Show extremely dry wit

parts.note: to show up is to come

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A performance full of very dry humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like the theatre piece in the scene, but it is the verb, as in turning up.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedy and wit both mean humour, the quality of being amusing.

clue.text: Tyrannical boss posted shifts

indicators.note: shifts means moves about, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bullying manager has put up the work rota.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler who wields power cruelly, a tyrant.

clue.text: American picked up, safe on dry land

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American

indicators.note: a sound picked up is heard, so the word is spelt to match how it is said

parts.note: safe as in certain, sure

explanation.surface: An American has been rescued and is safely back on land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' looks like a rescue in the scene; it signals that SURE and SHORE sound alike in British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashore means on or to the land rather than at sea.

clue.text: Cluttered tie rack becoming more gaudy

indicators.note: a cluttered space is in disarray, so these letters are jumbled up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tie rack crammed with ties looks ever more garish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacky means cheap and in poor taste, so tackier is more showy and vulgar.

clue.text: Son scratched by cutting instrument

indicators.note: something scratched is struck out, so this letter is removed

parts.note: sharp means able to cut
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A boy is scratched by a cutting tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' suggests a blade, but it is a musical one.
explanation.definitionFit: The harp is a stringed musical instrument plucked with the fingers.

clue.text: Walk when fit takes minutes

indicators.note: taking something in holds it inside, so the letter goes within

parts.note: able means fit, capable
M is the abbreviation for minutes

explanation.surface: A stroll, when you're healthy, only takes a few minutes.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, leisurely pace.

clue.text: Bowled over by Prince's first hit

parts.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone is bowled over by Prince's first hit record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' suggests a chart success for the singer Prince; it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A bop is a light punch or blow, so to bop is to hit.

clue.text: For example, played Under Pressure on piano a second time

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another follows it, so this piece goes after

parts.note: p is the musical marking for piano, softly
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second
T is the abbreviation for time
someone under pressure is tense

explanation.surface: Queen's hit Under Pressure was played again on the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitalised song title is a red herring: it simply means stressed. 'A second time' is not repetition but three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Played is a past-tense verb form, so it is an example of the past tense.

clue.text: Tar strengthened with vegetable matter?

parts.note: surface reading: road tar or pitch reinforced with plant fibre
setter's reading: a tar is a sailor, and this one grows strong by eating spinach, the cartoon hero

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tar' reads as the sticky black stuff; it is crossword-speak for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoon sailor gains superhuman strength whenever he eats a can of spinach, a vegetable.
